highlights.title: 'Sherlock Holmes Meets NCIS' Hit 2000s Detective Series Is Officially Free on Streaming
highlights.summary: The age of the great American cop show is over. Yes, franchises like NCIS and Law & Order are likely to continue until the heat death of the universe, but network TV used to be packed full of idiosyncratic crime-solvers, usually but not necessarily working hand-in-hand with local law enforcement.
body: Elementary is a modernization of the Sherlock Holmes story, which sets it in present-day New York City. When the show begins, Holmes (Jonny Lee Miller) is newly sober, following a stint in rehab for narcotics addiction, and has relocated from London to Manhattan.

Holmes' father, without consulting him, hires Dr. Joan Watson (Lucy Liu) to live with him as his "sober companion." Watson, a former surgeon turned addiction specialist, gets dragged along for the ride as Holmes pursues his only real passion: solving murders as a consultant for the NYPD.

Watching Elementary for the first time in 2026, it's one of the more entertaining depictions of Holmes. Miller plays him as brilliant but unfocused, and he’s consistently on thin ice with every person around him in one way or another. It's a far cry from the mellower Holmes of Arthur Conan Doyle's stories, but Miller's version is newly sober and recently traumatized. If you give it a few episodes, it does eventually make sense that Elementary 's Holmes is one big raw nerve.
points: The age of the great American cop show is over.

highlights.title: After 8 Years in Space, ‘BepiColombo’ Is Finally Approaching Mercury
highlights.summary: Following a difficult journey, the probe will soon begin unravelling the mysteries of Mercury’s magnetic field and internal structure.
body: BepiColombo has been on a bit of an Odyssey. The space probe—named after an acclaimed Italian scientist who developed the “gravity assist” trick that enables interplanetary journeys today—was originally scheduled to arrive at Mercury last year. However, after a malfunction with the propulsion, the probe was forced to change course so it could reach Mercury at reduced power. As a result, the arrival date was pushed back by nearly a year, and now after eight years in space, BepiColombo is beginning its descent to low orbit around Mercury.

On September 3, ground control confirmed that the propulsion module had successfully separated from the rest of the craft, marking the final phase of the joint mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). After a bumpy journey—reaching more than 200 million kilometers from Earth—transmissions from the probe indicated all went smoothly.

highlights.title: ‘Still feel a jolt of joy’: why Dirty Dancing is my feelgood movie
highlights.summary: The latest in our ongoing series of writers highlighting their most rewatched comfort films remembers a 1987 teenage girl classic. There is probably a Swedish word for the emotional state engendered in me by Dirty Dancing.
body: The movie must have seemed quite raunchy to me then. Light on actual sex, but heavy on petting during extended scenes of hot, fully-clothed couples grinding to a soundtrack of objectively incredible music. Catnip, then, for curious tweenage girls.

For several years, Dirty Dancing was the wallpaper to every sleepover I went to. Its catchphrases were social currency at my girls’ school. Shouting “I carried a watermelon,” or “nobody puts Baby in the corner!” across a crowded classroom signaled a nuanced understanding of the Year 7 zeitgeist. And, of course, we all tried to do the lift. So many memories of uniformed girls landing on top of other uniformed girls at break time; so many scraped knees and elbows.

highlights.title: World model companies are keeping a lot of secrets
highlights.summary: Everyone in the world-models space is sitting on a pile of cash and a ton of buzz, but good luck getting anyone — from the founders to their own data suppliers — to tell you what they're actually building.
body: This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale.

At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence, so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems.

But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.”

highlights.title: Three countries, one hike: an Alpine adventure in Austria, Slovenia and Italy
highlights.summary: The Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to stay. ‘Achtung! Staatsgrenze!” OK, the signpost marking the “state border” didn’t have exclamation marks but, with its no-nonsense Prussian font, it did…
body: Hikers hiked straight past. Mountain bikers used it to prop up their cycles. Cows grazed willy-nilly. And the patrons of the Schutzhütte Oisternig enjoyed their cold beers regardless of which country they were in. While official boundaries may have changed in these parts over the centuries, the magnificence of the mountains has not.

My husband and I had woken that morning in Austria, in the Carinthian village of Feistritz. After breakfast at the old Gasthof Alte Post, we’d bought a loaf from the bäckerei, climbed past the 15th-century church as its bells called worshippers for prayers and continued up through pine forest to these high Alpine meadows – and into Italy.

We started our journey by catching an early Eurostar to Amsterdam, where there was time for canals, beer and crispy bitterballen before boarding the Nightjet sleeper to Salzburg. In our adjoining capsule-like cabins, we watched the Netherlands segue into Germany, and woke at dawn to pasture, pines and peaks. On the final train from Salzburg to Villach, where we were beginning the loop, the Alps pressed closer, drawing us in.

highlights.title: Roman Sands RE:Build review – marooned in a crumbling vaporwave dream
highlights.summary: PC, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox; Arbitrary Metric The latest work from the team behind Paratopic is part compulsive time-loop management sim, part eerie subterranean adventure. Fetch the chair from storage. Deliver a message that causes disgust.
body: In this reimagining of the 2019 visual novel Roman Sands, crafted by the team behind the Americana horror road trip Paratopic, you’re trapped in a beach resort and tethered in a time loop. The task is deceivingly simple: fulfil menial directives from four gluttonous individuals, unlock tools and items to open more rooms and then do it all over again.

The loop is as monotonous as it sounds – and that’s the point. The visuals and sound work collide in flamboyant vaporwave-inspired story exposition. Reward animations are exaggerated to feed your lizard brain with dopamine, satirising the reward loops that make other games feel like a visit to a casino – some more maliciously than others. There’s gig economy commentary to boot.

Over time, I familiarised myself with everybody’s routine and needs. I was effective to the point of becoming uncomfortable about how entranced I was, squeezing every possible score multiplier out of every day so that I could spend fake money on stuff I didn’t need from a gachapon machine.
points: PC, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox; Arbitrary Metric The latest work from the team behind Paratopic is part compulsive time-loop management sim, part eerie subterranean adventure.

highlights.summary: Why is everyone talking about Mighty Mike Plays? From the (alleged) $118,000 bill to AI-generated T-shirt designs, we're here to explain how a Minecraft YouTube channel has captured the internet's attention.
body: It's a tale as old as time: a child is playing a video game, they grab their parent's credit card, and all of a sudden, someone has a thousand-dollar hole in their bank account. The story of Mighty Mike has so much in common with the lesson countless others have learned in the past – or does it?
Over the space of just a week, a nine-year-old YouTuber and his dad have ensnared an audience of millions, but not everyone is buying the events that started with a 14-minute Minecraft upload.

It's a sweet story that, apparently, as of September 14, started to come to an end. With a half-hearted "wassup chat" and a title that read " Message from Dad…Mighty Mike Plays is Over," it was clear the video lacked the same enthusiasm present in previous uploads. The channel's nine-year-old owner quickly signaled that the page would soon be shut down before handing the mic over to his dad, Dave, for an explanation.

highlights.title: A new start after 60: I’m 92 and cycling is my life – despite the crash that left me unconscious
highlights.summary: Arthur Plummer got a bike when he retired at 65 and joined a cycling club as one of its youngest members. Now he is its oldest but still racking up 5,000km every year. When Arthur Plummer retired at 65, he bought a secondhand bicycle.
body: “I love cycling,” he says. “Wherever I go, even if I ride on the same roads, there’s something new happening. When I get on my bike, I feel great. I come home at about 3pm and I feel exhausted. However, it’s the nicest feeling. It’s exhilarating, and it’s resulted in me being extremely healthy.”

Even when, in his late 80s, Plummer developed polymyalgia rheumatica (an inflammatory condition that causes pain, stiffness and inflammation in the shoulders, neck and hips) and was unable to walk, cycling helped him to move again. “I was in a wheelchair and I would sit outside in my driveway and people would go by and I felt trapped,” he says. “I can’t walk,” he thought, “but if I can get on my bike, I bet I could ride.” So that’s what he did.

Although his legs are strong, walking is still uncomfortable; he has a shortened stride and sometimes struggles to keep up with his wife and friends on holiday. Cycling, on the other hand, brings freedom. Plummer has cycled “on every street you can go on” within 100 sq miles (260 sq km) of where he lives. He often takes his bike on the bus so that he can explore farther afield. “I’m looking for new vistas,” he says.

highlights.title: ScrollEd wants to turn textbooks into TikTok
highlights.summary: ScrollEd turns textbooks into a scrollable, Instagram-like feed with video, audio, and quizzes. The Palo Alto startup, founded by student co-founders (and spouses) Utsav Gupta and Rebecca Neff, pitches at TechCrunch Disrupt.
body: Society has spent a lot of time bemoaning our digitally addled minds and goldfish-like attention spans, pointing the finger of blame at doomscrolling as the reason we can’t just sit down and read a book or study for exams. But what if the solution isn’t to stop scrolling, but to rethink what we’re scrolling through?

That’s the bet startup ScrollEd is making. The Palo Alto-based startup is pitching in the TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield 200 competition with the novel idea that if students won’t open a textbook, the textbook should open itself up to them — as a scroll.

ScrollEd has built an app that allows the user to turn any text file — including dry PDFs or text books — into a feed that feels a lot like Instagram Reels or TikTok. As you scroll, the content shows up as AI-generated video, audio, text, or even interactive quizzes. Swiping up surfaces a new topic, while swiping sideways lets you go deeper into the one you’re on, with a quiz waiting for you at the end.

“2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world,” Huang said in an interview with CBS News. “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.”

US lawmakers have criticised AI companies over the risks and Anthropic published a threat intelligence report detailing how criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have tried to use its powerful AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and spy on dissidents.

highlights.title: How many times has a player scored a hat-trick in a Premier League loss?
highlights.summary: Sunderland's Brian Brobbey scored the first hat-trick by a player on a losing side in the Premier League for 19 years - but how many others have done so?
body: Brian Brobbey etched his name in Premier League history on Sunday after scoring a hat-trick as part of the losing side.
The Netherlands striker is now only the fifth different player to do so in a Premier League match, after netting three times during Sunderland 's 5-3 defeat by Manchester City.
It is the first time that has happened in the top flight since 2007, and only the sixth time since the Premier League's formation in 1992.
The last player to achieve the feat was Roque Santa Cruz, scoring a hat-trick for Blackburn Rovers in a 5-3 defeat by Wigan Athletic in December 2007.

highlights.summary: Scottish breakfasts are worth getting up for: think eggs and potato cakes in a freshly baked roll, or toasted barley bread laced with sticky plums and honey butter. I’ve long wanted a space to cook the food that really excites me, and Clementine, which opens its doors in north London next month, is…
body: First, make the morning rolls. Combine the dry ingredients in a bowl, then rub in the lard. Add the water, mix to form a rough dough, then cover with a damp tea towel and leave to rest for 10 minutes.

Knead the dough until it feels smooth, springy and has good stretch – about 10 minutes in a mixer on medium speed, 25 minutes by hand. Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled container, cover with a damp tea towel and leave for about an hour to double in size.

Turn out the dough on to a well-floured surface, roll it into a rectangle, then divide into 12 equal pieces of about 120g each. Pinch the four corners of one piece of dough into the centre, then flip over. Allow the dough to stick slightly to the worktop and, with a cupped hand, work it into a tight ball. Now use a dough scraper to release it from the bench, then transfer to a lined, high-sided baking tray. Repeat with the remaining pieces of dough, spacing them evenly apart. Sprinkle each with a little flour, cover with a damp cloth and refrigerate overnight.
Heat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9, then bake the rolls for 25-30 minutes, until dark and “well fired” on top; remove and leave to cool slightly.

highlights.title: Humans, not rogue AI, are still the biggest cybersecurity risk to energy systems
highlights.summary: Before recent high-profile hacks raised the specter of AI possibly " killing all humans," our energy systems were already disturbingly vulnerable to cyberattack - and the risk is growing. "We were always prey.
body: “We were always prey. We were just kind of surviving at the appetite of our predators,” Joshua Corman, executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the Institute for Security and Technology (IST), told me last year. At the time, I was preoccupied with a Department of Homeland Security warning that Iranian actors and sympathizers could target the US with cyberattacks.

Last week, I called Corman up to chat about recent incidents of rogue AI agents orchestrating their own complex cyberattacks. Even AI executives are talking about whether the technology they’re building could grow so out of control that it triggers an apocalypse. If there is now a 10 percent chance of artificial intelligence one day killing all humans, as some AI developers warn, surely there’s a chance it could knock our lights out in the meantime?
“Any sociopath that wants to [attack] is now more powerful than they used to be.”

highlights.title: Silent Hill: Townfall Review
highlights.summary: Like the intravenous needle permanently jutting out of its hero’s wrist, Silent Hill: Townfall gives this long running series a welcome shot in the arm.
body: Things only get more alarming from there, but Townfall dragged me through its increasingly squeamish scenes with the powerful allure of its central mystery, which gradually brings to light the tragic events that have impacted the town, the main players at fault, and exactly where poor Simon stands in all of it. It’s a story that deals with familiar themes of trauma and guilt that we’ve come to expect from Silent Hill, but it also tackles previously unexplored shades of evil like corporate greed and environmental mismanagement that help to make it feel like a refreshingly new twist on the series’ formula.

Although he comes across as fairly monotone at first, I grew to appreciate the understated earnestness of Simon as the events of Townfall mine the full depths of his despair, especially compared to some of the overly dramatic heroes of the earlier Silent Hill games. At certain junctions, the story also switches the perspective to a couple of other playable characters that further flesh out the details of what’s really going on, but I’d rather not spoil exactly who they are other than to say that they provide crucial roles in unravelling St. Amelia’s secrets.
points: Like the intravenous needle permanently jutting out of its hero’s wrist, Silent Hill: Townfall gives this long running series a welcome shot in the arm.

highlights.title: Meta's Muse Is Better at Surveilling Than Helping Me
highlights.summary: The Muse app continues Meta’s trend of opting users into data collection for AI training. It also nudges you to share your bank account, email, and passport information.
body: I saw Meta’s latest app, Muse, cross-promoted on another Meta-owned platform, Instagram, and decided to download the AI assistant.

“Hand off everyday tasks like finding deals, booking reservations, and managing your inbox,” the pop-up read. “Muse keeps working while you get on with your day.” It’s free to use, and easily connects to other data sources, like my email and bank account. Muse’s default avatar is a beige-colored cross between an Ewok and a Labubu, with its arms outstretched, presumably to scoop up all my data.

Meta’s Muse is a mainstream version of AI agents already popular in Silicon Valley for automating personal tasks, like OpenClaw and Instinct. It’s a hit for the company: the Muse app has been downloaded over 900,000 times in its first week, according to Sensor Tower. The user experience is less like prompting a chatbot, and more like texting a friend with task requests—the AI agent acknowledges messages with a thumbs-up emoji and gets to work in the background. Muse is also available through Meta’s WhatsApp platform.
But after a few days with Muse, I’m convinced this AI tool is more obsessed with collecting data about me than actually getting stuff done.

highlights.title: ‘It’s about to go global’: American college football rocks into Wembley – a photo essay
highlights.summary: Our photographer, Tom Jenkins, captures the colour and razzmatazz as college football arrived in the capital, hot on the heels of successful NFL outings in recent years. Rarely has Wembley Way seen or heard such a commotion.
body: Pundits from Fox’s Big Noon Kickoff Show were broadcasting live from outside the venue – a curious spectacle in which the hosts even ate fish and chips in front of a fake Grenadier guard – as thousands of supporters around them waved placards and chanted college anthems. It fuelled a tailgate party atmosphere that wouldn’t have felt out of place in the States.

Dubbed the Union Jack Classic, the game pitted two sports-mad colleges, Kansas and Arizona State, against each other in front of 46,000 partisan fans, with many of the players one day hoping to play in the NFL.

“There’s a lot more grit and hunger in college football than in the NFL,” said Trey Latham, an ambitious 22-year-old linebacker for Kansas, on the eve of the clash. “College football teams go at it neck and neck. NFL players know they’re already fed, but we’re trying to feed our loved ones. There are scouts watching and people are desperate [to make it].”

The only previous college football game to be staged in the UK was in 1988, when Richmond beat Boston University at Crystal Palace. And while 42 NFL games have been staged in the UK capital over the past 19 years, college football has remained absent.

highlights.title: The agony of life with chronic body odour: ‘I swear I’ve tried every deodorant’
highlights.summary: Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferers. If Hayat goes out to eat, she’ll choose a table far away from other diners, ideally by a door or open window.
body: She chalks it up to a persistent past insecurity. “I still have that paranoia … It’s just in my head, because of everything I went through.”

For more than a decade, 66-year-old Hayat lived with bromhidrosis: chronic body odour. Though the term applies to BO from any cause, including poor hygiene, it is more typically driven by a bacterial imbalance or other health issue.

For those individuals, it’s not a question of bathing more often, or switching to a higher-strength deodorant: their body is working against them, and the impact can be ruinous. “Fifteen minutes after a shower, they’ve already started smelling,” says Chris Callewaert, a senior research fellow at Ghent University, Belgium, and one of the few scientists in the world specialising in body odour.

Callewaert describes bromhidrosis as a natural bodily process gone awry, most typically involving the apocrine glands. These are concentrated around the armpits, breasts and groin, and secrete lipids, steroids and proteins. This sweat itself is odourless; BO is produced by the natural bacteria on the skin and inside the hair follicles as they digest the fatty secretion.
points: Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferers.
If Hayat goes out to eat, she’ll choose a table far away from other diners, ideally by a door or open window.
